title: Lichen-feeding footmen moths increased faster than thermally matched moths in Britain 1993-2015 and Finland 1993-2022, but the Finnish site excess followed warming, not the local SO2 fall
abstract: We tested if lichen-feeding moths increased more than other moths with the same species temperature index (STI) while SO2 decreased, and if the excess was larger where modelled SO2 fell more. We used light-trap counts from 11 UK Environmental Change Network sites (1993-2015) and 62 Finnish monitoring sites (1993-2022), the 21 lichen-feeding species of Pescott et al. (2015), and EMEP MSC-W 0.1 degree SO2, NH3 and N deposition fields. At fixed STI, lichen feeders had abundance trends higher by 0.038 log units per year in Britain (95% site-bootstrap interval 0.024 to 0.106) and 0.027 in Finland (0.016 to 0.045). All nine model variants were positive, but with species as replicates the excess was only marginal (permutation p = 0.088 and 0.085; p = 0.003 in Finland 1993-2015). The footmen (Lithosiini) carried the excess; lichen feeders of other tribes did not increase. In Finland (53 sites, SO2 below 10 ug/m3 at all sites in 1993), the site excess was smaller where SO2 fell more (-0.036 per ug/m3, 95% CI -0.067 to -0.005; with latitude and warming -0.030, -0.072 to 0.011) and larger where sites warmed more (+0.18 per C per decade, 0.03 to 0.32). At 10 British sites the excess was larger where SO2 fell more (Spearman 0.49, p = 0.15), and the British increase came mostly after 2010. Thus the Finnish increase does not follow local SO2 recovery. The British data agree in sign with SO2 recovery but cannot separate SO2 from latitude. Limitations: few British sites, low Finnish SO2, modelled pollution, few species in one clade, and light-trap catchability.
